newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN OSTRICH WORKERS CATCH DEADLY CONGO FEVER.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN OSTRICH WORKERS CATCH DEADLY CONGO FEVER.

text.p: At least 17 people working at a South African ostrich abattoir are feared to have contracted the deadly tick-borne Congo fever and one of them has died, the abattoir operators said on Tuesday.
Congo-Crimean haemorrhagic fever is an infectious disease that like the more notorious viral disease Ebola causes body organs to degenerate with massive internal as well as some external bleeding.

The Little Karoo Cooperative, South Africa's leading producer of ostrich meat, hides and feathers, said in a statement that the abattoir in the eastern Cape town of Oudtshoorn had been closed as a precaution.
"The export of all fresh meat has been stopped immediately while all fresh meat supplies have been removed from butcheries where possible," the statement said.
About 30 percent of Congo fever cases are fatal.
A spokesman for the cooperative, Ben de Kock, said there were no recorded case of anyone being infected with Congo fever by eating ostrich meat.
"All the researchers are trying now to establish the source of infection," he said.
De Kock said the "perfect opportunity" for an abattoir worker to contract the disease was at the start of the slaughter line where some of the feathers are plucked by hand.
"If a tick gets squashed in the process, and the worker has an open cut or sore on his hand, the infection could spread," he said.

One of South Africa's top virus specialists, Bob Swanepoel, said infection could have spread during the processing of hides and feathers, when ticks would jump from the ostrich skins onto the human workers.

He said blood tests had so far confirmed Congo fever in four out of 16 patients transferred from Oudtshoorn to a Cape Town hospital since the weekend. One abattoir worker died before she could be transferred.
De Kock said another 10 of the total of 350 abattoir workers had been admitted to an Oudtshoorn hospital for observation on Tuesday after showing slight signs of fever.
South Africa's first confirmed case was in 1981 in a boy bitten by a tick and since then there have been sporadic cases, mainly in rural areas.
